questions.story: A leader broke out three weeks ago. It now sits 25% above its 50-day average, its widest stretch in a year. You missed the entry.
questions.q: What's the sound move now?
choices: Wait for a pullback or a new setup
Buy now before it runs further
Short it: it has to drop back
Buy half now and half on a dip
questions.answer: Wait for a pullback or a new setup
questions.why: Wait for a pullback or a new setup. The stock sits 25% above its 50-day average, its widest stretch in a year. ChartSchool calls a stock past its buy point a risky buy, because the advance has already begun. Its overview adds that after a big advance it may be prudent to wait for a pullback. Extended is not a reason to short: far above the average can be strength in a strong uptrend.
questions.lesson_line: An extended stock has already begun its advance. Wait for a pullback or a new setup.

wrong.Buy now before it runs further: That's chasing. ChartSchool calls a stock past its buy point a risky buy, because the advance has already begun.
wrong.Short it: it has to drop back: Far above the average can be strength in a strong uptrend. Extended is a reason to wait, not to short.
wrong.Buy half now and half on a dip: We don't scale in. Our rule is the full size at one price with one stop, no adding. ChartSchool calls a stretched buy risky.

questions.simple: Wait for a pullback or a new setup, because buying a stock this stretched means buying after the move began.

deeper.trap: The trap is fear of missing out. ChartSchool says a stock far above its average may be ripe for a pullback. After a big advance, it adds, waiting for a pullback may be prudent. Buying here means buying after the advance has already begun.

reasons: touches our no-chasing rules (rulebook C28, C29); the key agrees with them

questions.q: On the RSI, what reading is traditionally called overbought?
questions.why: RSI above 70. RSI moves between zero and 100. Wilder considered RSI overbought above 70 and oversold below 30, and ChartSchool, Investopedia and Fidelity give the same traditional levels. Investopedia words it as 70 or above. A reading of 50 is the middle of the scale, not an extreme.
questions.lesson_line: On RSI, 70 is the classic overbought line and 30 the oversold line.

wrong.RSI below 30: That's oversold, the other end of the scale.
wrong.RSI above 50: That's the middle of the scale, not an extreme. Overbought needs a high reading.
wrong.RSI above 14: 14 is the default look-back, the number of periods RSI uses. It's a setting, not an overbought level.

questions.simple: Above 70 is overbought, the classic line on the RSI scale, while below 30 is oversold.

questions.q: An overbought RSI reading means the stock is about to fall.
questions.why: False. Overbought means RSI is above 70: the stock has risen far and fast. ChartSchool says momentum gauges can become overbought and stay that way in a strong uptrend. Its glossary says overbought is not the same as bearish, only that a pullback might be due. Fidelity notes RSI can stay overbought for extended periods during strong trends.
questions.lesson_line: In a strong uptrend, overbought can stay overbought. I don't short a leader on RSI alone.
questions.simple: False, because in a strong uptrend RSI can stay overbought for a long time while price keeps rising.

deeper.trap: The trap is shorting a leader because RSI says overbought. Investopedia notes that RSI works best in trading ranges, not trending markets. In a strong trend the gauge can sit above 70 for extended periods while price climbs. Overbought says the stock has run, not that it is done.

questions.story: A stock has been in a steady downtrend for months. Its RSI drops to 25. A friend says it's oversold, so it has to bounce.
questions.q: What's the better read?
choices: It can stay oversold for a long time
Oversold means it is time to buy now
RSI 25 means the downtrend has ended
It should bounce once RSI nears 20
questions.answer: It can stay oversold for a long time
questions.why: It can stay oversold for a long time. RSI below 30 is the traditional oversold line, so 25 qualifies. Investopedia says an oversold condition can last a long time, and a rally may not come soon, or at all. It calls oversold an alert, not a buy signal. Many traders wait for price to start moving up before buying.
questions.lesson_line: Oversold is an alert, not a buy signal. Falling stocks can look cheap all the way down.

wrong.Oversold means it is time to buy now: Investopedia says some traders wrongly read oversold as a buy signal. It's more of an alert.
wrong.RSI 25 means the downtrend has ended: A reading doesn't end a trend. Price ends it, with a higher low and then a higher high.
wrong.It should bounce once RSI nears 20: No reading promises a bounce, not even a lower one. Investopedia says an oversold rally may not come soon, or at all.

questions.simple: It can stay oversold for a long time, because a weak stock can keep falling while its RSI stays low.

deeper.trap: Investopedia warns that stocks that keep falling look cheap all the way down. In a strong downtrend, Fidelity's slides note, an oscillator can stay in its oversold zone and give many false signals on the bounces. Let price show the turn first: a higher low, then a higher high above the last peak.

questions.q: What does the RSI measure?
choices: A stock's recent gains vs losses
A stock's move vs the S&P 500
questions.answer: A stock's recent gains vs losses
questions.why: A stock's recent gains vs losses. ChartSchool builds RSI from three parts: RS, average gain and average loss, over 14 periods by Wilder's default. Fidelity says RSI compares recent gains to recent losses, usually on a 0 to 100 scale. Investopedia says it compares a stock's strength on up days with its strength on down days.
questions.lesson_line: RSI weighs a stock's own recent gains against its own recent losses.

wrong.A stock's move vs the S&P 500: RSI looks at one stock alone. Investopedia says it compares the stock's up days with its own down days.
wrong.Today's volume vs average volume: That's relative volume. RSI uses price changes only.
wrong.Price vs its 200-day average: That's distance from a moving average. RSI uses the size of up moves and down moves.

questions.simple: RSI measures a stock's own recent gains against its own recent losses.

questions.q: In chart talk, what does relative strength compare?
choices: A stock's move vs a benchmark
Its price today vs a year ago
questions.answer: A stock's move vs a benchmark
questions.why: A stock's move vs a benchmark. ChartSchool's price relative is a ratio chart comparing one security with another. Fidelity says it is often used against a market index. Investopedia uses it to find stocks that outperform the market or a chosen benchmark. The CMT Association notes it has nothing to do with the RSI.
questions.lesson_line: I want stocks beating the market, not just rising with it.

wrong.Price vs its moving average: That's distance from an average. Relative strength compares the stock with a second security, such as an index.
wrong.Its price today vs a year ago: That's the stock against its own past. Relative strength compares it with a second security, such as a market index.

questions.simple: It compares a stock's move with a benchmark, such as a market index, to see if it beats the market.

questions.q: In chart talk, what is a leader?
choices: The biggest company in its industry
The stock with the highest share price
questions.why: A stock outperforming the market. ChartSchool's glossary defines a leader as an industry or company outperforming the market. A relative strength chart against the stock's group shows whether it is leading or lagging its peers. In business talk, Investopedia's market leader is the company with the largest market share, a different meaning.
questions.lesson_line: Leaders are found by performance, not by fame. Check how the stock moves against the index.

wrong.The biggest company in its industry: That's the business meaning, market share. On a chart, a leader is the stock beating the market.
wrong.The most heavily traded stock: Volume shows activity, not leadership. A busy stock can still lag the market.
wrong.The stock with the highest share price: A share price says nothing about performance. A leader is judged by its returns against the market, not by what one share costs.

questions.simple: A leader is a stock doing better than the market, judged by how it moves, not by its size.

deeper.trap: The trap is the business meaning. Investopedia's market leader is the company with the largest market share. On a chart, ChartSchool's leader is an industry or company outperforming the market.

questions.story: Over one month, the S&P 500 falls 8%. Stock A falls 2%. Stock B falls 15%.
questions.q: Which stock showed relative strength?
choices: A: it fell less than the index
Neither: you'd need each RSI first
questions.answer: A: it fell less than the index
questions.why: A. Relative strength compares a stock with a benchmark. ChartSchool's price relative rises when a stock advances more than the S&P 500 or declines less. A fell 2% while the index fell 8%, so A held up better. B fell 15%, which is relative weakness. ChartSchool adds that stocks holding up best in a decline are often the leaders when the market turns.
questions.lesson_line: Watch who holds up when the market drops. That's where the next leaders hide.

wrong.B: it fell the most: Falling more than the index is relative weakness.
wrong.Neither: both went down: Relative strength is about the gap to the index, not the direction. A fell far less than the market.
wrong.Neither: you'd need each RSI first: Relative strength is not the RSI. The CMT Association says RSI rates one stock alone, while relative strength compares two.

questions.simple: Stock A, because it fell less than the index, and holding up better than the market is relative strength.

deeper.example: Relative strength is a comparison, so a falling stock can show it. With the index down 8% and A down 2%, A's ratio to the index rises even as A's price falls. When the market turns, ChartSchool says, the stocks that held up best are often the leaders. Watch them first.

questions.q: Price makes a higher high, but RSI makes a lower high. Which word fits?
questions.why: Bearish divergence. ChartSchool defines it as price recording a higher high while the indicator forms a lower high, and Investopedia calls it negative divergence. Fidelity says a new high that RSI does not confirm can signal a price reversal. It is a warning, not a sell signal on its own: ChartSchool says to confirm RSI signals with other tools.
questions.lesson_line: Divergence is a yellow light. Wait for price to confirm before you act on it.

wrong.Bullish divergence: That's the mirror: a lower low in price with a higher low in the indicator.
wrong.Golden cross: That's two moving averages crossing, not price against an indicator.
wrong.Trend confirmation: Confirmation would be RSI making a higher high too. Fidelity says a new high that RSI does not confirm is a divergence that can signal a reversal.

questions.simple: It's bearish divergence, because price rose to a new high while the momentum behind it made a lower high.

questions.q: In a strong uptrend, bearish RSI divergences give many false signals.
questions.why: True. ChartSchool warns that divergences are misleading in a strong trend: a strong uptrend can show numerous bearish divergences before a top materializes. Fidelity's slides add that in some strong trends an oscillator stays in its zone and gives many false signals on corrections. A divergence is a warning to watch, not proof of a top.
questions.lesson_line: One divergence in a strong leader is a note, not an exit. Let price break first.
questions.simple: True, because a strong uptrend can show many bearish divergences while the stock keeps going up.

deeper.trap: The trap is selling a strong leader on the first bearish divergence. ChartSchool says a strong uptrend can show numerous bearish divergences before a top materializes, and each one can look like the end. Let price confirm before you act.

reasons: statement reworded by the final checker: the 'does not prove' wording was a negated-absolute tell

questions.q: A stock trades 3,000,000 shares today. Its 50-day average volume is 1,200,000 shares. What is its relative volume?
questions.why: 2.5x. Relative volume is today's volume divided by the average: 3,000,000 / 1,200,000 = 2.5. ChartSchool: an RVOL of 2.5 means volume is 2.5 times normal. A value of 1.0 means volume matches the average.
questions.lesson_line: Relative volume compares today with normal. A reading of 1.0 is a normal day; 2.5 is two and a half times normal.
questions.simple: It's 2.5x, because today's 3,000,000 shares divided by the 1,200,000 average is two and a half times normal.

wrong.0.4x: Flipped it: divided the average by today's volume.
wrong.25.0x: Decimal slip: moved the point one place too far.
wrong.1.5x: Used the extra volume over average, not today's volume itself.

questions.q: When a chart shows heavy volume on a day, what does that mean?
choices: Far more shares traded than usual
The price moved a lot that day
It was the most traded stock that day
questions.answer: Far more shares traded than usual
questions.why: Far more shares traded than usual. Volume counts the shares traded in a period, and heavy means well above the stock's own average. Every share bought is also a share sold, so volume alone does not say buyers beat sellers. It is not the size of the price move either: Schwab notes volume can rise with no rise in price.
questions.lesson_line: Volume is the crowd. Heavy volume means a lot of people cared about that day.

wrong.The price moved a lot that day: Price and volume are separate measures. A big move can come on light volume, and a quiet day on heavy volume.
wrong.Buyers outnumbered sellers that day: Every share bought is a share sold. Heavy volume means more shares changed hands, not more buyers than sellers.
wrong.It was the most traded stock that day: Heavy is judged against the stock's own average, not other stocks. Investopedia reads bars higher than average as high volume.

questions.simple: Heavy volume means far more shares than usual changed hands that day, compared with the stock's own average.

questions.story: A stock in a strong uptrend dips 6% over four days. Volume on the dip runs well below its 50-day average.
questions.q: How does the light volume read?
choices: Volume doesn't matter on a dip
questions.why: Likely just a pullback. ChartSchool says a pullback with low relative volume is likely just a pullback. Heavier than usual volume on the drop would show traders committed to a new downtrend. Schwab adds that a decline without above average volume implies investor concern is limited. Likely is not certain: the read changes if heavy volume shows up on further selling.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet dips in a strong trend are normal. Loud dips get my attention.

wrong.Big sellers are taking over: Big sellers leave heavy volume behind. This dip is quiet.
wrong.Volume doesn't matter on a dip: It matters a lot. Schwab reads a decline without heavy volume as limited concern.
wrong.Likely weak demand ahead: Light volume on the way down means sellers aren't pressing. Schwab reads a decline without above average volume as a sign that concern is limited.

questions.simple: It's likely just a pullback, because light volume on the dip shows few people are rushing to sell.

questions.q: A huge volume spike after a long run-up confirms the uptrend will keep going.
questions.why: False. A volume spike late in a long run-up does not confirm more gains. Schwab notes high volume can signal the end of a trend, the final surge before it is exhausted. ChartSchool says relative volume spiking to 4.0 or more, especially when overbought, could foreshadow a reversal. A moderately above-average reading is different: ChartSchool says it points the other way.
questions.lesson_line: After a long run, the loudest day can be the last one. Respect it.
questions.simple: False, because after a long run a huge volume spike can mark the last burst of buying before the trend ends.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading the loudest day as the strongest proof. Early in a move, rising volume can show traders are committed, Schwab says. After a long run, the same burst can be the last buyers rushing in. Investopedia's blow-off top is a steep rise in price and volume, followed by a steep, rapid drop.

questions.q: When a stock goes parabolic, what is the price doing?
questions.why: Rising faster and faster. Schwab describes parabolic as a rapid, accelerating rise in price. On a Fidelity webinar, the trend line under such a move has to be redrawn steeper and steeper. Investopedia's blow-off top shows how it can end: a near-vertical climb, then a steep, rapid drop.
questions.lesson_line: Parabolic moves speed up as they go. When they end, the drop can be steep and fast.

wrong.Drifting sideways on low volume: That's a quiet range, the opposite of parabolic.
wrong.Falling in a steady channel: That's a downtrend between two parallel lines.
wrong.Gapping down at the open: A gap down is a one-day jump lower. Parabolic is a run higher that keeps speeding up.

questions.simple: Parabolic means the price is rising faster and faster, so the climb keeps getting steeper.

questions.q: On a chart, what is a base?
choices: A one-day gap up on heavy volume
A steady climb with no pauses
The lowest point on the chart
questions.why: A sideways range lasting weeks. ChartSchool describes basing as a flat trading range without any noticeable trend, a stock catching its breath. Bulkowski's flat base is a price area the stock touches again and again over several weeks or months. How bases are built and judged is a later lesson.
questions.lesson_line: A base is a stock catching its breath. Learn to spot the flat stretch before the next move.

wrong.A one-day gap up on heavy volume: A gap is a single jump. A base takes weeks to build.
wrong.A steady climb with no pauses: That's a trend. A base is the pause.
wrong.The lowest point on the chart: That's one price, not a stretch of time. A base is a flat range that lasts weeks.

questions.simple: A base is a flat stretch where price moves sideways for weeks with no clear trend.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Big investors buying shares quietly while the price moves sideways is called ___.
questions.why: Accumulation. ChartSchool defines it as buying shares without making the price rise much. Schwab explains why: big investors want large positions but cannot buy all at once without pushing the price up. So the chart can look flat and dull while shares change hands. After a decline, ChartSchool says, a stock may base and trade sideways for a long time.
questions.lesson_line: A dull, flat chart can hide big buyers. That's why I keep watching quiet bases.
questions.simple: Accumulation, because big buyers spread out their buying so the price stays flat while they collect shares.

questions.q: On a chart, what does distribution mean?
choices: Selling that barely moves the price
Buying that barely lifts the price
A company paying out a cash dividend
A one-day crash on panic selling
questions.answer: Selling that barely moves the price
questions.why: Selling that barely moves the price. ChartSchool defines distribution as systematic selling that does not move the price much. Schwab says one hallmark is volume rising with no rise in price. On a chart the word has nothing to do with dividends. It is not a crash either: the price barely moves while the shares change hands.
questions.lesson_line: Heavy volume with no price progress is a warning. Someone may be selling quietly.

wrong.A company paying out a cash dividend: That's a different, business use of the word. On a chart, distribution means quiet selling.
wrong.Buying that barely lifts the price: That's the opposite: buying shares without pushing the price up much.
wrong.A one-day crash on panic selling: A crash is fast and loud. ChartSchool defines distribution as selling without significantly affecting the price.

questions.simple: Distribution is steady selling that barely moves the price, even while a lot of shares trade.

questions.q: When traders say a stock is trading tight, its price swings are small.
questions.why: True. Tight means a narrow range with small swings. Investopedia describes a sideways market as prices staying within a tight range. Schwab notes quiet markets make smaller bars. John Bollinger, quoted by ChartSchool, says low-volatility periods are often followed by high-volatility ones.
questions.lesson_line: Tight is quiet. Quiet stretches are often followed by bigger moves.
questions.simple: True, because tight means the stock trades in a narrow range with small swings.

questions.story: For three weeks a stock's swings keep shrinking: lower highs, higher lows. Volume dries up. It's coiled in the middle of its range.
questions.q: What does the coil tell you about the next move?
choices: A move may come; direction unknown
It most likely breaks out upward
It will break down through the low
It will stay quiet for months
questions.answer: A move may come; direction unknown
questions.why: A move may come; direction unknown. ChartSchool calls the narrowing pattern a coil: lower highs, higher lows, and volume that dries up, the quiet before the storm. John Bollinger notes low volatility is often followed by high volatility, and ChartSchool says narrowing bands give no directional clues. The direction of the breakout can only be determined after the break.
questions.lesson_line: A coil tells you to get ready, not which side to pick. Let the break choose.

wrong.It will break down through the low: Same guess the other way. ChartSchool says the direction is only known after the break has occurred.
wrong.It will stay quiet for months: Low-volatility stretches are often followed by high volatility. That's why traders watch coils.
wrong.It most likely breaks out upward: The story gives no trend for the coil to continue. ChartSchool says the breakout's direction can only be determined after the break.

questions.simple: A move may be coming, but the coil does not tell you which way, so let the break decide.

deeper.trap: The trap is guessing the side early. A coil looks ready to pop, and buying before the break bets on a direction the chart has not shown. ChartSchool notes the pattern usually forms as a continuation pattern, yet says the direction can only be known after the break.

reasons: only ChartSchool uses the word coil (see conflicts)

questions.q: What is a stock's 52-week high?
choices: Its highest price in the past year
Its highest price since it listed
Its average price over the past year
Its highest close of the past week
questions.answer: Its highest price in the past year
questions.why: Its highest price in the past year. Investopedia: a 52-week high is simply the highest price seen over the last year. ChartSchool's new highs count uses the same 52-week look-back. It is not the all-time high: a stock can make a 52-week high and still trade below older peaks.
questions.lesson_line: A new 52-week high means buyers are paying more than at any time all year. That's strength.

wrong.Its highest price since it listed: That's the all-time high. A 52-week high only looks back one year, so a stock can still sit under older highs.
wrong.Its average price over the past year: That's an average, not a high. The 52-week high is the single highest price in that year.
wrong.Its highest close of the past week: A week is far too short. The look-back is 52 weeks, a full year.

questions.simple: It's the highest price the stock reached in the past 52 weeks, which is one year.

questions.story: Stock A just closed at a new 52-week high. Stock B trades 30% below its 52-week high after a long slide.
questions.q: Which faces less selling from trapped buyers above it?
questions.why: A. At a new 52-week high, almost nobody who bought in the past year is holding a loss. B sits 30% under its high, so a year of buyers sits above it. ChartSchool explains that trapped buyers often sell near breakeven when price returns, which forms resistance. New highs, it adds, show buyers willing to pay even higher prices.
questions.lesson_line: At a new 52-week high, almost nobody from the past year is underwater. Far below the high, a trapped crowd waits.

wrong.B, after its slide: Cheaper isn't lighter. Every buyer between B's price and its high is a possible seller on the way back up.
wrong.They face the same: B has a year of trapped buyers above it. A has almost none from the past year.
wrong.Neither: losers just hold: Trapped buyers do sell. ChartSchool says many take the chance to escape near their cost with little to no loss.

questions.simple: Stock A, because at a new 52-week high almost no buyer from the past year is sitting on a loss.

deeper.counter: A new 52-week high clears overhead supply only from buyers inside that window. A stock can sit at a 52-week high and still trade below a peak from years ago, where older buyers wait. Look at the longer chart too. The claim here covers the past year, which is all a 52-week high tells you.

questions.q: A stock's high is $80. It now trades at $68. How far down from its high is it?
questions.why: 15%. Subtract the price from the high, then divide by the high: (80 - 68) / 80 = 15%. Measure from the high, not from today's price. We read every chart this way, in percent down from highs, so stocks at any price compare fairly.
questions.lesson_line: We read a chart in percents: down from highs, extended from the averages. Percents compare across stocks.
questions.simple: It's 15% down, because you measure the drop from the $80 high, not from today's price.

deeper.trap: The trap is dividing by the wrong number. Divide the drop by today's $68 and you get a bigger figure than 15%. The stock then looks further from its high than it is. Always divide by the high.

wrong.17.6%: Divided the $12 drop by today's $68, not by the $80 high.
wrong.12.0%: Used the $12 drop as a percent and never divided.
wrong.85.0%: $68 is 85% of the high. That is what is left, not the drop.

questions.q: On a daily chart, what makes a gap down?
choices: Today's high is below yesterday's low
Today's low is above yesterday's high
Today's range is smaller than usual
questions.answer: Today's high is below yesterday's low
questions.why: Today's high is below yesterday's low. ChartSchool and Bulkowski both define a down gap this way. The two days' price ranges do not overlap, so an empty space shows on the chart. A lower close alone is not a chart gap. Bulkowski notes gaps are useful for showing support or resistance zones.
questions.lesson_line: A gap down leaves a hole above the price. Gaps often mark support or resistance zones.

wrong.Today closes below yesterday's close: That's just a down day. On a chart, a gap needs empty space between the two days' ranges.
wrong.Today's range is smaller than usual: That's a narrow day. A gap is about the space between days, not the size of one.

questions.simple: A gap down is when today's whole range sits below yesterday's low, leaving empty space on the chart.

reasons: fixed before; gap has a second sense in V.05 (our Kicker), see conflicts

questions.q: An upward breakaway gap usually gets filled within a week.
questions.why: False. Bulkowski's figures for upward gaps: 85% of area gaps closed within a week, but only 1% of breakaway gaps did. ChartSchool says the adage that all gaps eventually get filled might not always hold true, especially for breakaway and runaway gaps. It warns that waiting for them to fill can devastate a portfolio.
questions.lesson_line: Don't sit out a strong breakaway gap waiting for a fill. It may never come.
questions.simple: False, because Bulkowski found only 1% of upward breakaway gaps closed within a week.

deeper.counter: Bulkowski's numbers cover one week. They say an upward breakaway gap rarely closes within a week, not that it never closes. Don't count on a fill, especially after a breakaway or runaway gap.

reasons: numbers that can change: Bulkowski's statistics (re-read 2026-11-12, still 85% and 1%)
statement reworded in wave8 to break the lesson's absolute-means-False pattern

questions.q: Which word is this: a gap late in a long move, on heavy volume, that closes within days as the trend ends.
questions.why: Exhaustion gap. ChartSchool: after a long move, a gap in the direction of the move is an exhaustion gap. To count, prices should reverse soon after and close the gap. Bulkowski: it happens at the end of a trend on high volume and usually closes within a week. So the label is often clear only after the gap closes.
questions.lesson_line: A huge gap after a long run can be the last gasp. Watch whether it closes.

wrong.Breakaway gap: A breakaway gap starts a new trend as price leaves a consolidation area. This gap came as a trend ended.
wrong.Common gap: Common gaps form inside quiet ranges, not at the end of a long trend.
wrong.Continuation gap: That one forms in the middle of a move, not as the trend ends.

questions.simple: It's an exhaustion gap, the last jump at the end of a long move that soon closes as the trend ends.

deeper.trap: The trap is calling it early. A tall gap on heavy volume late in a run can be a continuation gap or an exhaustion gap. ChartSchool says an exhaustion gap counts only if prices reverse soon after and close the gap. So the label is often clear only in hindsight.

questions.story: A stock broke out of a base weeks ago and has climbed almost straight up. Today it gaps up again on heavy volume. For weeks after, it keeps making new highs and never comes back to the gap.
questions.q: Which gap type fits best?
questions.why: Runaway gap. It came weeks into a straight-line advance, and price kept making new highs without closing it. Bulkowski calls this a continuation gap, and ChartSchool also calls it a measuring gap. An exhaustion gap also comes late on heavy volume. But it is usually not followed by new highs, and it tends to close within a week. A breakaway gap starts the move as price leaves a base.
questions.lesson_line: A gap mid-trend that never fills is strength. Don't wait for it to close before you trust the trend.

wrong.Exhaustion gap: An exhaustion gap is usually not followed by new highs and tends to close fast. This one did the opposite.
wrong.Breakaway gap: A breakaway gap starts the move as price leaves a base. This one came weeks into the run.
wrong.Common gap: Common gaps form in quiet, trendless stretches and close within days.

questions.simple: A runaway gap, because it came in the middle of a fast climb and price kept making new highs without filling it.

deeper.trap: On the gap day itself, a runaway gap and an exhaustion gap can look alike. Both come after a long run, often on heavy volume. Bulkowski tells them apart by what follows: exhaustion gaps usually close within a week, while continuation gaps see new highs without closing. Here, weeks of new highs settled it.

questions.story: A stock ran from $10 to $80 in two years. On your chart, the move from $10 to $20 looks the same size as $70 to $80.
questions.q: What would show the $10 to $20 move as the bigger one?
questions.why: Log scale. A log scale measures moves in percent. $10 to $20 is a 100% gain, while $70 to $80 is a much smaller one. On an arithmetic scale every dollar takes the same space, so the two moves look equal. Changing the timeframe or the chart type does not change how price is spaced.
questions.lesson_line: On long charts and big movers, use log scale. Percent is what your account feels.

wrong.A shorter timeframe: Zooming in changes the window, not how price is spaced. The scale is the fix.
wrong.An arithmetic scale: That's the scale you're on. It spaces every dollar the same, so $70 to $80 looks as big as $10 to $20.
wrong.A line chart instead: A line chart joins the closing prices. It changes how price is drawn, not how the price axis is spaced.

questions.simple: A log scale, because it spaces moves by percent, and $10 to $20 is a far bigger percent gain.

questions.q: Today's high is $52.40 and today's low is $50.10. What is the day's range?
questions.why: $2.30. ChartSchool defines the daily range as the day's high minus the same day's low: $52.40 - $50.10 = $2.30. On a bar chart, Schwab notes, the height of the bar shows that range. It is not the change from yesterday's close.
questions.lesson_line: Range is the day's high minus its low, the distance between the two.
questions.simple: It's $2.30, the high minus the low for the day.

wrong.$102.50: Added the high and the low instead of subtracting.
wrong.$51.25: Took the midpoint of the day, not the range.
wrong.$23.00: Decimal slip: moved the point one place up.

questions.q: A stock rallies from $40 to $60, then pulls back to $50. What percent of the rally has it given back?
questions.why: 50%. Divide the drop from the top by the size of the rally: (60 - 50) / (60 - 40) = 50%. Dow Theory's Hamilton estimated that pullbacks retrace 1/3 to 2/3 of the prior move, with 50% being typical. ChartSchool's glossary adds that a retracement of more than 2/3 typically signals a trend reversal. These are rules of thumb from history, not guarantees.
questions.lesson_line: Measure a pullback as a share of the rally. Past two-thirds, ChartSchool says a reversal is more likely.
questions.simple: It gave back 50%, half the rally, because it fell halfway from $60 back toward $40.

wrong.200.0%: Flipped it: divided the rally by the pullback.
wrong.83.3%: Gave the $50 price as a share of the $60 top.
wrong.125.0%: Gave the $50 price over the $40 start.

questions.q: The S&P 500 peaks at 5,000 and falls to 4,400. How far is it down from the peak?
questions.why: 12%. Divide the drop by the peak: (5,000 - 4,400) / 5,000 = 12%. Investopedia calls a decline of 10% or more from the peak a correction. By that line, this drop is a correction.
questions.lesson_line: Measure a drop from the peak. A fall of 10% or more counts as a correction.
questions.simple: It is down 12%, past the 10% line Investopedia uses for a correction.

wrong.1.2%: Decimal slip: moved the point one place too far.
wrong.6.4%: Divided the drop by the two levels added together.
wrong.0.1%: Divided the drop by the peak and never made it a percent.

questions.q: Generally, a bear market means a broad market index has fallen 20% or more over at least two months.
questions.why: True. Investor.gov is the SEC's site for investors. It says a bear market generally means a broad market index falls by 20% or more over at least a two-month period. It also describes a bear market as a time of falling prices and pessimistic sentiment. The word generally matters: this is a rule of thumb, not a law.
questions.lesson_line: A 20% drop from the peak in a broad index is the usual line for a bear market.
questions.simple: True, the SEC's investor site says a bear market is generally a 20% or more drop over at least two months.

reasons: one cited fact only (Tier 1); Investor.gov returned 403 to WebFetch on 2026-11-12 (confirmed by the checker on 2026-11-09)

questions.q: Which word is this: you act on a buy signal, and the price reverses against you within days.
questions.why: Whipsaw. ChartSchool defines it as a buy or sell signal that is reversed in a short time. Investopedia says you are whipsawed when price abruptly moves the other way right after you buy. Volatile markets and sensitive indicators can cause whipsaws.
questions.lesson_line: Whipsaws are a cost of trading signals. Volatile markets and sensitive indicators can cause them.

wrong.Accumulation: Accumulation is big buyers quietly building positions in a range.
wrong.Breakaway gap: A breakaway gap is a gap that starts a new move.
wrong.Golden cross: A golden cross is a shorter moving average crossing above a longer one.

questions.simple: A whipsaw, because the buy signal reversed against you in a short time.

questions.q: How do you draw an uptrend line?
choices: Draw a flat line at the lows
questions.why: Connect the rising lows. ChartSchool says an uptrend line has a positive slope and joins two or more lows. Two points draw it, and a third touch confirms it. A line over the rally peaks is the channel line, the upper edge. Murphy's laws on ChartSchool add that a line tested more often matters more.
questions.lesson_line: Uptrend lines go under the lows. The more clean touches, the more the line matters.

wrong.Connect the rising highs: In an uptrend, a line over the rally peaks is the channel line, the upper edge.
wrong.Connect the closing prices: That's a line chart, not a trendline.
wrong.Draw a flat line at the lows: A flat line at the lows marks support. An uptrend line slopes up: ChartSchool says it has a positive slope.

questions.simple: Connect the rising lows, because an uptrend line runs under the dips and slopes upward.

questions.q: When price breaks below an uptrend line, the uptrend has reversed.
questions.why: False. A break of an uptrend line is a warning, not a verdict. ChartSchool says trend line breaks should serve merely as a warning that a change in trend may be imminent. It says to check a break with support and resistance levels or peak and trough analysis. By Dow Theory, an uptrend stays in place until a lower low forms. Investopedia says only that a break could indicate a reversal, and that many false signals occur.
questions.lesson_line: A broken trendline says pay attention. A lower low says the uptrend is done.
questions.simple: False, because a broken trendline is only a warning, and the uptrend holds until price makes a lower low.

deeper.trap: The trap is acting on the line alone. ChartSchool says to validate a trend line break with horizontal support and resistance or peak and trough analysis. By Dow Theory, an uptrend is in place until a lower low forms and the decline exceeds the previous low. Check the swing lows before you call the trend over.

reasons: sources differ in strength (Murphy: usually signals), see conflicts

questions.q: In its first few days, a reversal can look exactly like an ordinary pullback.
questions.why: True. Investopedia says there is no perfect way to tell a pullback from a reversal. For a few critical sessions, they look identical. Its reversal page says the same. Dow Theory adds that investors often mistake a counter-move for the start of a new trend. Only later price action sorts them out.
questions.lesson_line: You won't know at the start. That's why our stop goes in first, before you find out.
questions.simple: True, because at the start a reversal and a pullback move the same way, so you cannot tell them apart.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading the first down days as proof either way. Investopedia says a pullback and a reversal look identical for a few critical sessions. Dow Theory warns that people often mistake a counter-move for a new trend. Only later price action sorts them out.

questions.q: What is a pullback?
choices: A short dip inside an uptrend
A change from uptrend to downtrend
A break above the last high
A slow sideways drift in price
questions.answer: A short dip inside an uptrend
questions.why: A short dip inside an uptrend. Investopedia calls a pullback a temporary dip in an otherwise rising stock price, before the price continues upward. Prices often pull back to trend lines, and in Investopedia's examples to near the 50-day moving average, before rebounding. A pullback ends with the uptrend resuming; a lasting change of direction is a reversal.
questions.lesson_line: Pullbacks in strong uptrends are one of the two classic places to buy. A new high is the other.

wrong.A change from uptrend to downtrend: That's a reversal. A pullback is temporary, and the uptrend carries on.
wrong.A break above the last high: That's a breakout, price clearing a level that held it. A pullback is a dip, not a push higher.
wrong.A slow sideways drift in price: That's a sideways market, prices staying in a tight range for a long period. A pullback is a dip lower, and then the uptrend resumes.

questions.simple: A pullback is a short dip in a stock that is still in an uptrend, and then the rise goes on.

reasons: fixed before; pullback has a second, narrower sense in Bulkowski (see conflicts)

conflicts: Pullback vs throwback: Bulkowski (glossary, throwbacks page) and Fidelity's Kirkpatrick slides call a return to the breakout price after an UPWARD breakout a 'throwback' and keep 'pullback' for the return after a DOWNWARD breakout. Investopedia, ChartSchool's moving-average page and everyday usage call any short dip inside an uptrend a pullback. The unit uses the everyday meaning for pullback (q63, q39) and teaches throwback only in Bulkowski's sense (q17); no question asks which side of a breakout a 'pullback' follows.

Exhaustion gap: ChartSchool (glossary G and the gaps article) and Bulkowski agree it is a gap IN the direction of a long move, near its end, closed soon. Investopedia's gap page describes it as 'a break lower in prices (usually on a daily chart) that occurs after a rapid rise'. q52 keys the ChartSchool/Bulkowski version; Investopedia's wording is not used.

What counts as a gap: ChartSchool and Bulkowski define it by the whole range (today's high below yesterday's low for a down gap). Investopedia also counts a 'partial gap' (an open beyond the prior close but inside the prior range) and defines a 'full gap' by the open. q50 uses the full-range definition from the two that agree.

Correction: ChartSchool's glossary (C) defines a correction technically, as a decline that retraces 1/3 to 2/3 of an advance. Schwab and Investopedia use the index convention: a decline of more than 10% from a peak (Schwab adds 'but less than 20%'; Investopedia gives no upper bound). q57 asks only for the computed percent and words the 10% line as the convention 'most people use'.

Leader: ChartSchool's glossary defines a leader as an industry or company outperforming the market, and an Interactive Brokers webinar by Dan Russo, CMT, says relative strength shows whether a stock 'is leading or lagging its peers'. Investopedia's 'Market Leader' page is the business meaning (largest market share). Nasdaq's leaders-vs-laggards articles and investors.com refused both clients, and Investopedia's CAN SLIM page (read from the Internet Archive) muddles O'Neil's L ('Laggard stocks are preferred ... Use the relative strength index'), so neither was used. q33 keys the chart meaning and names the business meaning in the reveal.

Base: ChartSchool's 'Basing' is a flat trading range after a decline; growth-stock usage (O'Neil, IBD) also calls a consolidation after an advance a base; Bulkowski's flat base is a flat price area touched repeatedly over weeks or months. q42 keys only the shared part: a sideways range lasting weeks or more, with no clear trend. Base anatomy is V.04's job.

Coil: only ChartSchool (symmetrical triangle page) names the narrowing pattern a 'coil'; I found no second Tier 2 publisher using the word. q46's key does not rest on the word: it rests on the point two publishers agree on, that a narrowing range gives no clue to direction (ChartSchool triangle and squeeze pages; Investopedia sideways market: the old trend may continue or a new one start).

52-week high: Investopedia's 52-week page says the figure is 'based on the security's daily closing price'; ChartSchool and Investopedia's breakout page speak of the highest price. Data vendors differ. q47's answer ('its highest price in the past year') holds either way, and no question asks close vs intraday.

Breakout: Investopedia, ChartSchool and Bulkowski count a break below support as a (downside) breakout; most traders call it a breakdown, as Investopedia itself notes ('a downside breakout, often called a breakdown'). q12 keys 'a move through resistance or support' so neither reading is marked wrong; q13 keys breakdown, and its word bank leaves 'breakout' out so the downside reading cannot make a second right answer.

Extended: ChartSchool's glossary measures it from the pivot (buy point); IBD's well-known 5% buy-zone rule was not used because investors.com refuses this tool's crawler. Our own usage (owner: '% extended from MAs') measures it in percent above the moving averages. q25 and q26 are asked as ours (house: true) with ChartSchool's distance-from-moving-average method as the Tier 2 backing.

RSI levels: ChartSchool notes some traders move the levels to 80/20 and short-term traders use other settings. q28 asks only for the traditional level (Wilder's 70/30, stated by ChartSchool, Investopedia and Fidelity).

Relative strength vs RSI: Investopedia's 'Relative Strength' page discusses RSI as a companion tool in the same article, which blurs the two. ChartSchool's Price Relative page (a ratio against a benchmark) and both RSI pages (average gain vs average loss of the stock itself) keep them apart; q31 and q32 follow those.

Existing bank skill vocab.chart (29 chart-picture items: trending, downtrend, coiled, higher lows, inside day, gapping, heavy volume, near its highs, at the 20 EMA, pullback) is not repeated: this unit asks words in text form, and where it reuses a word (pullback, heavy volume, coiled, uptrend) it asks a different thing about it. Inside day is left to V.03 (candle words).

Trendline breaks: Murphy's 10 laws on ChartSchool (f233) say a break 'usually signals a change in trend'; ChartSchool's trend lines page says a break is 'merely a warning that a change in trend may be imminent', and Investopedia that it 'could indicate' a reversal. q61's statement is absolute ('the uptrend has reversed'), which is false under all three, so its key stands; f233 is kept here and not cited in q61, so the reveal never seems to argue with its own key. ChartSchool's glossary T says the same as Murphy ('The breaking of a trend line usually signals a trend reversal'); 'usually signals' is still not 'has reversed', and ChartSchool's trend lines page shows a break that did not reverse the trend.

Death cross: Investopedia's page refuses every client this checker has (WebFetch, curl, the quote checker).
